question: For $$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$$ and $$B=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{bmatrix},$$ calculate $AB$ and $BA$ and then expand $(A+B)^2$ using matrix multiplication to establish why the scalar identity $(A+B)^2=A^2+2AB+B^2$ cannot be used for these matrices.
explanation:
Examination of Commutativity

We have $$AB=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$$ whereas $$BA=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$$ Thus, $AB\ne BA$, showing that multiplication of these matrices is not commutative.

Expansion of the Square

By the distributive property, $$(A+B)^2=(A+B)(A+B)=A^2+AB+BA+B^2$$ Now, $$A^2=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{bmatrix},\quad B^2=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{bmatrix}$$ Therefore, $$A^2+AB+BA+B^2=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{bmatrix}$$ $$=\begin{bmatrix}5&4\\4&5\end{bmatrix}$$ Directly, $$A+B=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$$ so $$(A+B)^2=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5&4\\4&5\end{bmatrix}$$ However, $$A^2+2AB+B^2=\begin{bmatrix}6&4\\4&4\end{bmatrix}$$ which is different because $AB\ne BA$. Hence, for these matrices the correct expansion is $A^2+AB+BA+B^2$, and the usual scalar form with $2AB$ is not valid.
